criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban water supply for human consumption available to the inhabitants of colonial Santiago de Chile (1541-1810), including river channels/acequias, public fountains, wells, and water carriers.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 because it discusses colonial institutional, legal, administrative, and governance arrangements for urban water supply (the cabildo, alcaldes/jueces/tenientes de aguas, mercedes de agua, public-works taxes such as derramas, sisa, and ramo de balanza, and Bourbon administrative reforms). Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because it provides a macro-historical administrative overview of municipal public-works financing and overlapping colonial jurisdictions rather than empirically analysing a specific rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (mentioning turns/tandas and cutoffs under mercedes de agua only in passing from secondary legal histories). Regardless of the Criterion 2 reading, the paper fails Criterion 3 (no empirical evidence).
criterion_notes.c3: Narrative historical essay synthesizing secondary historical literature (e.g., Calvo 1901, Piwonka 1999, Dougnac 1984/1985, De Ramón 2000). Contains no empirical research design, no primary archival or empirical data collection, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis; excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Narratively describes city-wide water availability, interruptions caused by floods and earthquakes (e.g., 1609, 1647, 1783), and chronic water insecurity in colonial Santiago, summarizing supply sources by period in Table 1 from secondary works.
criterion_notes.c5: No identifiable empirical study design, sample, or analytical unit linking an exposure to a measured household/community access outcome; purely a narrative administrative history essay.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish with an English abstract; Spanish is directly readable and feasible to translate under Criterion 10, so the record is assessed substantively rather than excluded on language grounds.

evidence_quotes.quote: This article aims to analyze water supply for human consumption during the colonial period in Santiago de Chile. Using the concept of governance as a reference framework, this work characterizes water supply sources available to the inhabitants of the city, the institutions in charge of managing their access, and the destructive impact that some natural phenomena, such as floods and earthquakes, had in the infrastructure designed for that purpose.

El objetivo de este trabajo es analizar el abastecimiento de agua para consumo humano en el Santiago colonial, identificando sus fuentes de origen, los aspectos institucionales que impactaron en su gobernanza y las problemáticas que impidieron la consolidación de un sistema que proporcionara agua de forma constante y segura a los habitantes de la ciudad.

Esta utilización estaba sometida a regulaciones que disponían el ejercicio y uso de las aguas a través, por ejemplo, de turnos o tandas para facilitar el acceso equitativo al recurso y que, en caso de incumplirse, podían llegar al corte o la suspensión del suministro.
Fuente: Elaboración propia a partir de Calvo (1901) y Piwonka (1999).

Si bien las autoridades de la época llevaron adelante distintas iniciativas tendientes a satisfacer las necesidades básicas de consumo de agua, es posible identificar al menos tres factores que dificultaron que el complejo desafío de captar, conducir y distribuir el líquido de forma permanente y segura pudiera concretarse para beneficio de los santiaguinos.

raw_response.exposure: Colonial institutional governance (cabildo, Bourbon reforms), public-works financing taxes (derramas, sisa, ramo de balanza), and natural disasters
raw_response.outcome: Historical availability, continuity, and quality of urban drinking water supply in colonial Santiago
raw_response.population_and_sample: Inhabitants of colonial Santiago de Chile (1541-1810); no empirical sample
raw_response.rationale: This Spanish-language article is a narrative administrative and historical overview of urban drinking water supply in colonial Santiago de Chile (1541-1810) based entirely on secondary historical literature, with no empirical methods, no primary archival or empirical data, and no systematic empirical synthesis (E05). In addition, while it satisfies the plain wording of Criterion 2 by discussing colonial governance institutions, it focuses on macro-historical institutional jurisdiction and public-works financing rather than analysing a specific rule-type mechanism governing household service access under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading; under both readings of Criterion 2, it is excluded for lack of empirical evidence.
raw_response.study_design: Narrative historical essay based on secondary literature (non-empirical)
